'''Vishnu''' (vish′nö), ''n.''   [< Skt. ''Vishnu''.]   ''Hind. myth.'', the god who with the oth great gods, Brahma and Siva, forms the tr or trinity; the Preserver, considered worshipers to be the supreme god of the Hindu pantheon. {{smaller|In the Vedas he appears only as a manifestation of the sun. The myths relating to Vishnu are chiefly characterized by the idea that whenever a great disorder affected the world Vishnu descended to set it right. Such descents are called ''avatâras'' or ''avatars'', and consist in Vishnu’s assuming the form of some wonderful animal or superhuman being, or as being born in human form of human parents, and always endowed with miraculous power. These avatars are generally given as ten, nine of which are already past, the tenth, the ''Kalki-avatâra'', being yet to come, “when the practices taught by the Vedas and the institutes of the law shall have ceased, and the close of the ''Kalí'' or present age shall}}
{{smaller|be nigh.” Vishnu is sometimes represented as Garuda, a being half bird and half man; as holdi of his four hands a conch-shell blown in battle, i a disk as emblem of supreme power, in the thir as the emblem of punishment, and in the fourt as a type of creative power.}}

[[File:century v08 p0574 c1f1.png|center|60px]]
{{c|{{smaller|Vishnu. (From Moo Pantheon.”}}}}

'''visibility''' (viz-i-bil′i̤-ti), ''n.''   [< F. ''visi'' Sp. ''visibilidad'' = Pg. ''visibilidade'' = It. ''vi'' < LL. ''visibilita(t-)s'', the property or cond being seen, < ''visibilis'', visible: see ''visib'' The state or property of being visible, ceivable by the eye; perceptibility; th of being exposed to view; conspicuous
{{smaller block|Sir Richard Browne [during nineteen years’ e kept up in his chapel the liturgy and offices of th of England, to his no small honour, and in a tim was so low, and as many thought utterly lost, th ous controversies, both with Papists and Secta divines us’d to argue for the ''visibility'' of the Chu his chapel and congregation.
{{right|''Evelyn'', Diary, Ju}}}}
'''2†.''' A thing which is visible.
{{smaller block|The ''visibility'' [of the Holy Ghost] being on an e of visible light. Quoted in ''Walton’s'' Complete An}}

'''visible''' (viz′i-bl), ''a.'' and ''n.''   [< ME. ''visible'', < OF. (and F.) ''visible'' = Sp. ''visible'' = Pg. ''visivel'' = It. ''visibile'', < LL. ''visibilis'', that may be seen, < L. ''videre'', pp. ''visus'', see: see ''vision''.]   '''I.''' ''a.'' '''1.''' Perceivable by the eye; capable of being seen; open to sight.
{{smaller block|<poem>Then the eighteth sone borne of Melusin,
Thre eyes hauyng on in front ''uisible;''
Moche peple meruellyd and wonderd ther-in.</poem>
{{right|''Rom. of Partenay'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 1269.}}}}
{{smaller block|Were armies to be raised whenever a speck of war is ''visible'' in our horizon, we never should have been without them.
{{right|''Jefferson'', Works, VIII. 69.}}}}
'''2.''' Apparent; open; conspicuous: as, a man with no ''visible'' means of support.
{{smaller block|Though his actions were not ''visible.''
{{right|''Shak.'', Cymbeline, iii. 4. 152.}}}}
{{smaller block|The factions at court were greater, or more ''visible'', than before.
{{right|''Clarendon.''}}}}
'''3.''' In ''entom.'', noting parts which are not concealed by other parts, as the spiracles when they are not concealed under the hard parts of the integument: opposed to ''covered''.—{{smaller|'''Visible church''', in ''theol.'', the church of Christ on the earth; the whole body of professed believers in Christ.—'''Visible horizon''', the line that bounds the sight. See ''horizon''.—'''Visible means''', means or resources which are apparent or ascertainable by others, so that the court or a creditor can ascertain that the person is responsible or reach his property.—'''Visible spectrum.''' See ''spectrum'', 3.—'''Visible speech''', a name applied by Prof. A. Melville Bell, its inventor, to a system of alphabetical characters designed to represent every possible articulate utterance of the organs of speech. The system is based on a penetrating analysis of the possible actions of the speech-organs, each organ and every mode of action having its appropriate symbol.='''Syn.''' Discernible, in sight, obvious, manifest, clear, distinct, evident, plain, patent, unmistakable}}.
'''II.''' ''n.'' That which is seen by the eye.
{{smaller block|''Visibles'' work upon a looking-glass, which is like the pupil of the eye.
{{right|''Bacon'', Nat. Hist., § 263.}}}}
{{smaller block|Go into thy room and enter into that spiritual communion which is beyond all ''visibles''.
{{right|''A. E. Barr'', Friend Olivia, iii.}}}}

{{right|''Scott.''}}}}

{{right|''Galt'', Steam-Boat, p. 143. (''Jamieson.'')}}}}

'''vision''' (vizh′on), ''n.''   [< ME. ''vision'', ''visioun'', ''visiun'', < OF. ''vision'', F. ''vision'' = Sp. ''vision'' = Pg. ''visão'' = It. ''visione'', < L. ''visio''(''n''-), the act or sense of seeing, vision, < ''videre'', pp. ''visus'', see, = Gr. ἰδεῖν (*Ϝιδεῖν), Skt. √ ''vid'', know, = E. ''wit'': see ''wit''<sup>1</sup>. From the L. ''videre'' are also ult. E. ''visible'', ''visage'', ''vis''<sup>1</sup>, ''visit'', ''visive'', ''visual'', ''advice'', ''advise'', ''device'', ''devise'', ''pervise'', ''revise'', ''supervise'', ''provide'', ''provision'', ''revision'', ''supervision'', etc., ''evident'', ''provident'', ''evidence'', ''providence'', etc., ''purvey'', ''survey'', etc., ''invidious'', ''envy''<sup>1</sup>, etc.]   '''1.''' The act of seeing external objects; sight.
{{smaller block|Faith here is turned into ''vision'' there.
{{right|''Hammond'', Practical Catechism, i. § 3.}}}}
'''2.''' The faculty that perceives the luminosity, color, form, and relative size of objects; that sense whose organ is the eye; by extension, an analogous mental power. As noting one of the five special senses of the body, ''vision'' is correlated with ''olfaction'', ''audition'', ''gustation'', and ''taction''. See ''sight''<sup>1</sup>.—'''3.''' That which is seen; an object of sight; specifically, a supernatural or prophetic appearance; something seen in a dream, ecstasy, trance, or the like; also, an imaginary appearance; an apparition; a phantom.
{{smaller block|There duelled the Holy Prophete Daniel; and there he saughe ''Visiounes'' of Hevene.
{{right|''Mandeville'', Travels, p. 43.}}}}
{{smaller block|Your old men shall dream dreams, your young men shall see ''visions''.
{{right|Joel ii. 28.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Departing Year! ’twas on no earthly shore
My soul beheld thy ''vision!''</poem>
{{right|''Coleridge'', Ode to the Departing Year, iv.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Far in the North, like a ''vision'' of sorrow,
Rise the white snow-drifts to topple and fall.</poem>
{{right|''R. T. Cooke'', September.}}}}

'''4.''' Anything unreal or imaginary; a mere creation of fancy; a fanciful view.
{{smaller block|''Visions'' of dominion and glory rose before him.
{{right|''Macaulay'', Hist. Eng., vi.}}}}

{{smaller|'''Arc of vision''', in ''astron.'', the arc measuring the sun’s distance below the horizon when a star or planet previously concealed by his light becomes visible.—'''Axis of vision.''' See ''axis''<sup>1</sup>.—'''Beatific vision''', in ''theol.'' See ''beatific.''—'''Binocular vision''', vision effected by the coöperation of both eyes in such a way that the two impressions made upon the retinæ are perceived as one; stereoscopic vision. It is by means chiefly of binocular vision that we are enabled to judge of the relative positions of objects.—'''Center of vision.''' Same as ''point of vision.''—'''Chromatic vision''', a condition of sight in which objects appear to have a color they do not possess, or to have an iridescent border; chromatopsia.—'''Day-vision''', a condition of sight in which vision is weakened or lost at night; night-blindness; hemeralopia.—'''Dichromic vision''', a form of color-blindness in which there is perception of but two of the primary colors; dichromism. In this condition the perception of red is usually wanting.—'''Direct''' or '''central vision''', the formation of the sight-image at the macula lutea.—'''Direct-vision spectroscope.''' See ''spectroscope.''—'''Double vision''', the perception of two images of one and the same object; diplopia.—'''Erect vision.''' See ''erect.''—'''Field of vision.''' See ''field.''—'''Indirect''' or '''peripheral vision''', formation of the sight-image at some part of the retina other than the macula lutea.—'''Intuitive vision.''' Same as ''beatific vision.''—'''Iridescent vision''', a condition of sight in which objects appear to be bordered with alternating colors like those of the rainbow: a form of chromatopsia.—'''Limit of distinct vision.''' See ''limit.''—'''Night-vision,''' a condition of vision in which objects are perceived more clearly at night; day-blindness; nyctalopia.—'''Persistence of vision.''' See ''persistence.''—'''Point of vision.''' See ''point''<sup>1</sup>.—'''Reflected vision, reflex vision.''' See ''reflex.''—'''Refracted vision,''' vision performed by means of rays refracted or deviated by passing through mediums of different densities.}}

'''vision''' (vizh′ọn), ''v. t.''   [< ''vision, n.'']   '''1.''' To see as in a vision; perceive by the eye of the intellect or imagination.
{{smaller block|<poem>We in the morning eyed the pleasant fields
''Vision’d'' before.</poem>{{right|''Southey'', Joan of Arc, viii.}}}}
{{smaller block|Such guessing, ''visioning'', dim perscrutation of the momentous future!
{{right|''Carlyle'', Past and Present, ii. 8. (''Davies.'')}}}}
'''2.''' To present in or as in a vision.
{{smaller block|It [truth] may be ''visioned'' objectively by representatives and symbols, when the prophet becomes a seer, . . . ''visioned'' as out of the mind, . . . now as actual water ''visioned'' and flowing clear.
{{right|''E. H. Sears'', The Fourth Gospel, The Heart of Christ, pp. [72, 80.}}}}

'''visional''' (vizh′ọn-a̤l), ''a.''   [< ''vision'' + ''-al.'']   Of or pertaining to a vision; seen in a vision; hence, not real. ''Waterland.''

'''visionally''' (vizh′ọn-a̤l-i), ''adv.'' In a visional manner; in vision.
{{smaller block|''Visionally'' past, not eventually.
{{right|''Trapp'', On Rev. xi. 14, quoted in Biblical Museum, V.}}}}

'''visionariness''' (vizh′ọn-ā-ri-nes), ''n.'' The character of being visionary.
{{smaller block|Dulness from absolute monotony, and ''visionariness'' from the aërial texture of the speculations.
{{right|''De Quincey'', Style, iii.}}}}

'''visionary''' (vizh′ọn-ā-ri), ''a.'' and ''n.''   [= F. ''visionnaire'' = Sp. Pg. It. ''visionario''; as ''vision'' + ''-ary''.]   '''I.''' ''a.'' '''1.''' Apt to behold visions; of powerful and foreseeing imagination; imaginative; in a bad sense, apt to receive and act on mere fancies or whims as if they were realities; given to indulging in day-dreams, reveries, fanciful theories, or the like.
{{smaller block|<poem>No more these scenes my meditation aid,
Or lull to rest the ''visionary'' maid.</poem>
{{right|''Pope'', Eloisa to Abelard, l. 162.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>The Sonnet glittered a gay myrtle-leaf
Amid the cypress with which Dante crowned
His ''visionary'' brow.</poem>
{{right|''Wordsworth'', Misc. Sonnets, ii. 1.}}}}

'''2.''' Of or pertaining to visions; of the nature of a vision or a product of the imagination; imaginary; in a bad sense, having no real basis; not founded on fact or possibility; impracticable; impossible: as, a ''visionary'' scheme.
{{smaller block|<poem>Some things like ''visionary'' flights appear;
The spirit caught him up, the Lord knows where.</poem>
{{right|''Dryden'', Abs. and Achit., i. 656.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>O Sleep, why dost thou leave me?
Why thy ''visionary'' Joys remove?</poem>
{{right|''Congreve'', Semele, ii. 2.}}}}
{{smaller block|Men come into business at first with ''visionary'' principles. ''Jefferson'', To Madison (Correspondence, II. 325).

That the project of peace should appear ''visionary'' to great numbers of sensible men . . . is very natural.
{{right|''Emerson'', War.}}}}

'''3.''' Appropriate to or characterized by the appearance of visions.<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
